lede: The tasks people bring to AI models account for 23 percent of US wages, pay has stayed within its usual range while the mix of jobs has shifted more than in any three years since 2013, and 42 percent of new degrees are in fields that lead to the most exposed jobs.
meaning: The tasks people bring to AI models are paid about a quarter of all the wages in the United States, while pay across the skills behind them has moved no further over the last three years than in an ordinary stretch of the record, so these models already reach a wide share of paid work and there is no sign yet that employers pay for those skills differently.

The reading that stands out is the mix of work: over the last three years employment has moved toward jobs that draw on arts and humanities by more than in any three-year stretch since 2013, although a record of thirteen years produces a shift that size by chance about one time in eleven, and the same test was passed in 2020, when the pandemic reshuffled employment, so the next release of the wage tables will show whether it holds.

What employers ask for moved before the models did: within occupations, job ads named the tasks the models can do less often from 2020 to the third quarter of 2022, and the release itself added a step of 2.6 standard errors against the 5.4 needed to stand out from an ordinary month.

Degrees are the slow channel and the one policy can count: 41.8 percent of new bachelor's degrees in 2025 went to the most exposed third of fields, against 40.7 percent in 2024, and people who move into those jobs from other occupations will join the count once the flows between occupations are published.

bridge.how: Each conversation in the usage record is matched to the O*NET tasks it touches, each task is weighted by the wages paid for it in the latest OEWS release, and the share moves with every usage release, every few months, for the one platform whose record the index reads so far. A task counts as reached when any use of it is published, so the headline comes from the latest release that publishes every task, and the tasks making up three quarters of use are counted in every release alike, since no release leaves any of them out.

city.how: For each skill group the index takes the last three yearly changes in pay, and in the share of employment, and sets them against that group's own changes since 2013: a change stands out when it passes the level only the most extreme three-year stretches in the record reached, and both the reading and that level are recalculated with each spring release of the wage tables. The job-ad reading compares, within each occupation and month, the share of ads naming each task with that task's exposure, and sets the change at the release against the same change placed at every earlier month.

valley.how: Degrees come from the IPEDS completions file and each field of study is scored by the exposure of the occupations its graduates hold, on the task measure of Eloundou and coauthors, so the share moves once a year, and people who arrive in exposed jobs from other occupations will join this view when the flows between occupations are published.
